subject: History
title: The Middle Ages
learningOutcomes: Analyze the traits of ancient civilisations and the internal and external causes of the fall of the Western Roman Empire.
Explain the origin, chief characteristics, and social and economic impact of feudalism in medieval Europe.
Identify the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire and explain how it survived while the West fell.
Describe the distribution of authority in the Catholic Church and the dominance of religion during the Middle Ages.
Explain the rise of the Mongols and their impact on trade and Eurasian societies.
Explain the historical background of Jerusalem and the causes of the Crusades.

sections.heading: Introduction to Ancient Civilisations
sections.body: Many of the world's great civilisations began and flourished near rivers, because rivers gave people water, food from hunting and fishing, and fertile alluvial soil for farming. Rivers also acted as routes for trade. The four major early river-valley civilisations were the Mesopotamian civilisation (Tigris and Euphrates), Ancient Egypt (Nile), the Indus Valley civilisation (Indus), and the Chinese civilisation (Yellow or Huang He River). Surplus food supported large populations, cities, writing, and the growth of civilisation.

sections.heading: The Roman Civilisation
sections.body: The Roman civilisation grew in Europe near the Tiber River. Rome emerged around 753 BCE as a group of small villages on low hills that grew into self-governing city states. The Mediterranean Sea route connected Rome with other regions for trade, helping it grow wealthy. By 250 BCE Rome was a strong power controlling most of Italy, with a powerful army. The empire grew so large that around 284 CE the Emperor Diocletian split it into two halves — the Eastern and Western Roman Empires — because it had become too large to govern as one unit.

sections.heading: Reasons for the Fall of the Western Roman Empire
sections.body: Several problems caused the decline: the government became corrupt and a power struggle began; Constantine moved the capital to Constantinople, weakening Rome; the Church of Rome gained unlimited power; the army became weak; heavy taxes made ordinary people miserable and caused chaos; provinces rebelled and declared independence; and Barbarians and Huns from Central Asia attacked. In 476 CE the last Western Roman Emperor (Romulus Augustulus) was overthrown by the German chieftain Odoacer, marking the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

sections.heading: Origin of Feudalism and Medieval Europe
sections.body: Feudalism was a political, economic, and social system in medieval Europe based on land ownership and loyalty. It developed between the 10th and 13th centuries and became common in the 11th century, after the fall of Rome left a power vacuum. Society was arranged in a feudal pyramid of four hierarchies: Kings at the top (who owned all the land and answered only to the Church), then Nobles (tenants-in-chief), then Knights (also called lords, who followed the code of chivalry), and Peasants at the bottom, who did the farming.

sections.heading: The Chief Characteristics of Feudalism
sections.body: Kings received taxes, military aid, and sometimes food from their vassals, and in return the Crown protected them — the rule of 'give and take'. Land was granted in scattered pieces in different parts of the country to prevent any noble from growing powerful enough to rebel, so loyalty was very important. Every part of the system, from the crown to the peasants, depended on each other. The Church was also granted large lands and, as an independent institution, did not pay tax to the king. Farming used the Three Field System: one field grew wheat or rye, one grew spring crops such as peas and beans, and the third lay fallow to restore fertility, with the use rotated each year.

sections.heading: Impact of Feudalism
sections.body: From the 14th century feudalism began to weaken. The Black Death plague (1347–1352 CE) killed more than a quarter of Europe's population, causing a severe labour shortage so there were not enough peasants to work the land. The growing power of monarchy and nobility, and the rise of commerce and coin money, meant lords could be paid in money instead of military service. Trade flourished, peasants moved to towns to live freely, nobles became weaker, soldiers were paid wages, and centralised governments were established — ending the feudal era.

sections.heading: The Byzantine Empire
sections.body: Byzantium was a former Greek town with an important location on the Bosphorus, between Europe and Asia, where major trade routes met. Emperor Constantine rebuilt and fortified it and renamed it Constantinople (today Istanbul, Türkiye). The Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire survived the fall of the Western Roman Empire and lasted about a millennium (roughly 330 CE to 1453 CE), becoming one of the greatest and richest empires in Europe. Constantine was the first Roman Emperor to accept Christianity (Edict of Milan, 313 CE), and in 380 CE Christianity became the state religion under Emperor Theodosius I.

sections.heading: Distribution of Authority in the Catholic Church
sections.body: The Catholic Church had a clear hierarchy of authority. From top to bottom it ran: the Pope, then the Archbishop and Cardinals, then the Lesser Bishops and the Abbot of the monastery, and then the Priests and the Monks and Nuns. The Pope sat at the very top with supreme authority over all other Church officials and was regarded as more powerful than kings.

sections.heading: Dominance of Religion During the Medieval Period
sections.body: Religion dominated medieval life. In 1054 CE the Church of Constantinople and the Church of Rome split in the 'East–West Schism', dividing Christianity into the Roman Catholic Church (Western Europe) and the Eastern Orthodox Church (Eastern Europe). The Pope held supreme power over both the Church and the lives and politics of the people. His verdict on Heaven and Hell was absolute, and anyone — even a king — could be declared an outcast and excluded from the Christian community, which was called excommunication.

sections.heading: The Dark Ages
sections.body: The Dark Ages (or early Middle Ages) lasted from about 476 CE to 800 CE. Wide-scale warfare halted progress, and the Church controlled wealth and was the biggest landowner. People paid the Church a tithe — one-tenth of their income. Learning was limited and free thinkers were persecuted: scientists and thinkers hid their ideas for fear of the Church. The astronomer Galileo, who supported the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun, was tried by the Inquisition in 1633 and placed under house arrest, and Giordano Bruno was burned at the stake in 1600 — examples of how the Church suppressed ideas that challenged its authority.

sections.heading: The Mongols
sections.body: The Mongols were natives of Mongolia, a land of grasslands in Central Asia (north of China). They were nomadic tribes who reared cattle and moved from place to place in search of grazing pastures, and were feared as fierce raiders. Changez Khan (1162–1227 CE) founded the Mongol Empire, uniting the nomadic tribes by 1206 CE and building the largest contiguous land empire in history. In the 13th century the Mongols (the Golden Horde, under Batu Khan) invaded Eastern Europe; Ogedai Khan's forces conquered Hungary, Poland, Krakow, and Lublin, and were heading for Vienna when Ogedai died and the army returned, so the Mongols never conquered Western Europe. Despite their destructiveness, the Mongols contributed greatly to globalisation, connecting East and West and encouraging the exchange of trade, ideas, and technology.

sections.heading: The Holy City of Jerusalem
sections.body: Jerusalem has long held deep religious significance for Muslims, Jews, and Christians, and is considered holy by all three Abrahamic faiths because of the sacred sites and religious events associated with it. Caliph Hazrat Umar bin Khattab (RA) was the first Muslim ruler to bring Jerusalem under Muslim rule, in 638 CE. Muslims ruled the city for about 450 years while maintaining religious harmony, allowing pilgrims of other religions to visit their holy places — a policy of religious tolerance.

sections.heading: Background and Causes of the Crusades
sections.body: The situation in Jerusalem changed in 1009 CE when the Fatimid Caliph Al-Hakim created hurdles for Christian pilgrims, and worsened under the Seljuk Turks, who were less tolerant of Christian pilgrims. In response, Pope Urban II called on Christians (Council of Clermont, 1095) to retake the Holy Land. The Crusades were a series of wars between Christians and Muslims over control of Jerusalem, known as the 'War of the Cross', fought between about 1095 CE and 1270 CE. The First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099; the Muslim leader Salah ad-Din (Saladin) recaptured it in 1187; and although Crusaders won some battles, they ultimately failed to keep Jerusalem.

definitions.definition: An advanced human society with its own culture, government, laws, and way of life.
Fertile soil deposited by river water near riverbanks, ideal for growing crops.
A large group of territories controlled by a single ruler or government.
Independent cities that govern themselves, each with its own laws and army.
The Roman Emperor who split the empire into Eastern and Western halves (around 284 CE).
The leader or head of a tribe or clan.
The new capital built by Emperor Constantine, today known as Istanbul, Türkiye.
People considered uncivilised who did not belong to the major civilisations.
A nomadic group from Central Asia, known for violent raids, that helped cause Rome's fall.
A political, economic, and social system in medieval Europe based on land ownership and loyalty.
A system in which people are ranked one above another according to status or power.
The code of honour and conduct that knights had to follow.
A person who received land from a king or lord in exchange for loyalty and military service.
Land left uncultivated for a period so it can recover its fertility.
A deadly plague that spread through Europe in 1347–1352 CE, killing over a quarter of the population.
A system of government in which a king or queen rules as head of state.
A system where one central authority holds power, replacing local lords.
A former Greek town rebuilt by Constantine and renamed Constantinople.
A period of one thousand years.
Being officially excluded from the Christian Church and community as a punishment by the Pope.
A split or division within a group, especially a religious group.
One-tenth of a person's income paid to the Church as a religious tax.
A person who holds beliefs that contradict the official teachings of the Church.
Moving from place to place with no fixed home, to find food and pasture.
The process by which countries and peoples become connected through trade, culture, and communication.

interactiveLesson.instructions: Explore the medieval world. Select each part of society to continue.

hotspots.label: The King
hotspots.fact: The king sat at the top of the feudal pyramid. He owned all the land, answered only to the Church, and granted land to nobles in return for loyalty and military support.

hotspots.label: The Nobles
hotspots.fact: Nobles (tenants-in-chief) were granted land by the king. They governed their lands, collected taxes, kept local armies, and provided soldiers for the king.

hotspots.label: The Knights
hotspots.fact: Knights, also called lords, served the nobles and followed the code of chivalry. They fought in wars and were granted land in return for military service.

hotspots.label: The Peasants
hotspots.fact: Peasants did the actual farming. They were free or bonded: free peasants rented land and paid the lord, while bonded peasants worked the lord's land for a small piece of land in return.

hotspots.label: The Church
hotspots.fact: The Church was granted large lands but paid no tax. It grew enormously wealthy and powerful, and the Pope was regarded as more powerful than kings.

To hide from enemies in the water

practiceQuestions.prompt: Near which river did the Roman civilisation grow?

practiceQuestions.prompt: The Western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE.
practiceQuestions.explanation: In 476 CE the last Western Roman Emperor was overthrown.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In the feudal pyramid, the ____ were at the very top.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Kings sat at the top of the feudal hierarchy.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What code of conduct did knights have to follow?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Knights followed the code of chivalry.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What did Constantine rename the city of Byzantium?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Constantine rebuilt Byzantium and renamed it Constantinople.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The Pope was at the top of the Catholic Church hierarchy.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Pope held supreme authority over the Church.

practiceQuestions.prompt: ____ Khan founded the Mongol Empire and united the tribes.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Changez Khan founded and united the Mongol Empire.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why did the Mongols NOT conquer all of Western Europe?

They chose to stop at Vienna

practiceQuestions.explanation: When Ogedai Khan died, the army returned to Mongolia.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Jerusalem is considered holy by which three faiths?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Jerusalem is holy to Muslims, Jews, and Christians.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The word 'Crusades' means 'War of the Cross'.
Who called on Christians to launch the First Crusade?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Pope Urban II called for the First Crusade in 1095.

The Western Roman Empire falls (476 CE)

practiceQuestions.explanation: This is the timeline from Rome's founding to its fall.

items: The Western Roman Empire falls (476 CE)
Rome dominates most of Italy (250 BCE)
correctOrder: Rome dominates most of Italy (250 BCE)

sequencingActivity.explanation: Rome rose from a small settlement, dominated Italy, was split by Diocletian, and finally fell in 476 CE.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: How did moving the capital to Constantinople weaken the Western Roman Empire?

options: It shifted power and resources away from Rome, making the West harder to defend

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Moving the capital drew power and resources east, weakening the West.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Why did the Black Death help end feudalism?

options: It killed so many peasants that there were too few to work the land
It ended the Church's power overnight

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: The labour shortage from mass deaths broke the feudal system of land-based work.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Why were land grants scattered across different parts of the country?

options: So no single noble could gather enough power to rebel

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Scattering land stopped any noble from becoming powerful enough to rebel.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Why did the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire survive while the West fell?

options: Its strong, fortified capital and rich trade location kept it powerful for centuries

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Constantinople's defences and its wealthy trade position helped the East endure ~1000 years.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Which chain of events best explains what triggered the Crusades?

options: Hurdles for pilgrims under Al-Hakim, then harsher Seljuk rule, then Pope Urban II's call
A plague, then a famine, then a flood
The fall of the Mongols, then a schism
The death of Changez Khan, then a rebellion

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Restrictions on pilgrims and less tolerant Seljuk rule led Pope Urban II to call the First Crusade.
